text: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) (BASS). Objective: Determine how solid-material flame spread and suppression differ in microgravity versus Earth gravity, with an eye to spacecraft cabin atmospheres. Outcome: Published summaries describe sustained opposed-flow flame spread over thin cotton-fiberglass fabric in microgravity at cabin-like atmosphere, with concurrent-flow spread continuing after flow changes. Fuel: Cotton / PMMA (solid). Atmosphere: 21% O2 at 101 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Opposed & concurrent flow ≤ ~5 cm/s (fan duct). Hardware: ISS · Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) fan-driven flow duct. Years: 2010–2012 (approx.).

Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) — published finding: Flame spread over thin fabric persists in microgravity at cabin-like atmosphere — materials selection must assume forced-flow dependence [1].

Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) — published finding: Suppression behaviour studied in-flight: spread responds to flow direction changes (published summaries describe geometry-dependent burns) [1].

Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) variables swept: Opposed vs concurrent airflow; Flow speed; Sample configuration (thin/thick); Fuel material. Measurements recorded: Video flame spread; Flame shape & brightness; Suppression attempts (aerosol/flow); Sample regression. Fuel: Cotton / PMMA (solid). Atmosphere: 21% O2 at 101 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Opposed & concurrent flow ≤ ~5 cm/s (fan duct).
Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) materials/samples tested: Cotton-fiberglass fabric; PMMA (Plexiglas); Thick/thin solid samples.

Burning and Suppression of Solids – II (BASS-II) (BASS-II). Objective: Extend BASS to the low-flow / long-duration regime, where the balance between forced flow and buoyancy changes most dramatically in microgravity. Outcome: Published summaries describe very long-duration flame spread in extremely low flow, with fabric samples burning for many minutes and spreading behaviour changing slowly over time. Fuel: Cotton / PMMA (solid). Atmosphere: 21% O2 at 101 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Very low forced flow; long-duration burns. Hardware: ISS · MSG fan-driven flow duct (BASS hardware). Years: 2014–2017 (approx.).

text: Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (Saffire-I) (SAFFIRE-I). Objective: Study large-scale fire growth on a single ~0.4 × 1 m fabric sample in microgravity, at an overall size impossible to achieve inside the ISS, to enable prediction of fire growth in habitable volumes. Outcome: Published summaries describe the largest intentional spacecraft fire ever conducted, with the large fabric sample burning inside the enclosed instrumented flow duct. Fuel: Cotton-fiberglass fabric (solid). Atmosphere: 21% O2 at 101 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Duct flow ≈ 10–20 cm/s (approx.). Hardware: Uncrewed Cygnus cargo spacecraft · instrumented flow duct. Years: 2016 (approx.).
Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (Saffire-I) — published finding: Large-scale fire growth in microgravity was demonstrated and offered for material-response modeling [2].
Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (Saffire-I) — published finding: Saffire's scale bridges ISS bench-top fabric data to spacecraft-volume fire scenarios for model validation [2].

Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (Saffire-I) variables swept: Sample size (large scale); Flow speed; Duration of burn. Measurements recorded: Cinematic video imagery; Flame-spread extent; Heat release estimate; Temperature profiles. Fuel: Cotton-fiberglass fabric (solid). Atmosphere: 21% O2 at 101 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Duct flow ≈ 10–20 cm/s (approx.).
Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (Saffire-I) materials/samples tested: Cotton-fiberglass blend fabric (0.41 × 0.94 m, approx.).

Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (Saffire-II) (SAFFIRE-II). Objective: Burn nine distinct material samples (various spacecraft materials and thicknesses) in the same flow field so flammability can be compared across materials and related to small-scale tests. Outcome: Published summaries describe multiple smaller material samples burning in a single duct, allowing direct comparison between different spacecraft-relevant materials under identical conditions. Fuel: Mixed material samples (solid). Atmosphere: 21% O2 at 101 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Duct flow (instrumented). Hardware: Uncrewed Cygnus cargo spacecraft · instrumented flow duct. Years: 2016 (approx.).
Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (Saffire-II) — published finding: Direct flammability comparison between multiple spacecraft-relevant materials was collected under a single flow condition [2].
Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (Saffire-II) — published finding: Results connect individual small-scale material samples to large-scale fire-growth modeling for crewed volumes [2].

Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (Saffire-II) variables swept: Material identity; Thickness; Sample orientation; Shared flow field. Measurements recorded: Video of each sample; Heat flux & temperature estimates; Flame behavior per material. Fuel: Mixed material samples (solid). Atmosphere: 21% O2 at 101 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Duct flow (instrumented).

Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (Saffire-II) materials/samples tested: Cotton-fiberglass fabric; Nomex-type fabric; Kapton-type film; PTFE-type material; Other spacecraft polymers (mixed set of 9).

Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (Saffire-III) (SAFFIRE-III). Objective: Extend Saffire-I with a fire able to interact with changing conditions, providing evidence for how fires respond in scenarios closer to an unattended spacecraft fire. Outcome: Published summaries describe a final large-sample spacecraft fire with varied conditions phases, extending the Saffire-I evidence into deliberately changing upstream flow scenarios. Fuel: Cotton-fiberglass fabric (solid). Atmosphere: 21% O2 at 101 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Duct flow (varied across phases, approx.). Hardware: Uncrewed Cygnus cargo spacecraft · instrumented flow duct. Years: 2017 (approx.).
Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (Saffire-III) — published finding: Large-fire response to changing test conditions was demonstrated at serial scale [2].
Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (Saffire-III) — published finding: Completes the Saffire trilogy's data pool for spacecraft fire-growth modeling effort [2].

Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (Saffire-III) variables swept: Condition phases over burn; Flow variations; Sample scale. Measurements recorded: Video; Heat-release trend; Pressure/temperature telemetry. Fuel: Cotton-fiberglass fabric (solid). Atmosphere: 21% O2 at 101 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Duct flow (varied across phases, approx.).
Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (Saffire-III) materials/samples tested: Cotton-fiberglass fabric (large sample).

Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) (SAME). Objective: Characterize outgoing smoke particle sizes from overheated spacecraft materials to design next-generation smoke detectors that detect fires early in microgravity without false alarms. Outcome: Published summaries report particle size distributions from overheated spacecraft materials, showing smoke particle sizes vary strongly by source material and differ from Earth-based detector assumptions. Fuel: Overheated spacecraft materials (smoke). Atmosphere: — O2 at 101 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Quiescent smoke sampling. Hardware: ISS modal facility · smoke-generation sample oven + Fire Detection Modules (FDM). Years: 2006–2012 (approx.).
Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) — published finding: Smoke particle size differs strongly by source material (published summaries give material-specific distributions) [6].

Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) — published finding: Direct evidence supports re-designing smoke-detection thresholds around actual spacecraft smoke instead of Earth detector legacy [6].

Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) variables swept: Smoke source material; Overheating condition; Detector type. Measurements recorded: Particle size distribution (FDM); Count median diameter; Detector response comparison. Fuel: Overheated spacecraft materials (smoke). Atmosphere: — O2 at 101 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Quiescent smoke sampling.
Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) materials/samples tested: Teflon (PTFE); Kapton; Cotton; Cellulose; Silicone rubber (as smoke sources).

Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment – R (SAME-R) (SAME-R). Objective: Re-run SAME with refinements to gather a broader and more accurate dataset of smoke particle characteristics for spacecraft fire detection design. Outcome: Published summaries repeat the SAME measurements with updated instruments and additional materials, refining the particle-size evidence used for spacecraft detector design. Fuel: Overheated spacecraft materials (smoke). Atmosphere: — O2 at 101 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Quiescent smoke sampling. Hardware: ISS modal facility · SAME follow-on hardware. Years: Follow-on to SAME (approx.).

text: Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) (FLEX). Objective: Map how droplet flames extinguish in atmospheres diluted with N₂, CO₂ and He, providing the extinction-limit evidence needed to design flame-suppression atmospheres. Outcome: 276 tests charted droplet-burning extinction, burn time and burning rate across pressure, oxygen and gas-diluent conditions (Table IX of NASA/TP-2015-216046). Fuel: Methanol / heptane (droplets). Atmosphere: 20% O2 at 101 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Quiescent (still chamber). Hardware: ISS · Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) · Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA). Years: 2009–2011 (Table IX span).
Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) — published finding: Extinction boundaries measured across diluents — CO₂ and He show distinct suppression potency relative to N₂ [3].

Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) — published finding: Cool-flame behaviour observed in some methanol droplets after visible-flame extinction (published FLEX summaries describe 'cool flames') [3].

Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) variables swept: Fuel (methanol/heptane); Ambient pressure; O₂ concentration; Diluent (N₂ / CO₂ / He); Droplet diameter. Measurements recorded: Droplet diameter vs time (video); Extinction diameter; Burning rate; Burn duration; End-state classification. Fuel: Methanol / heptane (droplets). Atmosphere: 20% O2 at 101 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Quiescent (still chamber).
Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) materials/samples tested: Methanol droplets; Heptane droplets.

Flame Extinguishment Experiment – 2 (FLEX-2) (FLEX-2). Objective: Extend FLEX droplet extinction work to binary fuel mixtures and reconsider the role of the gas environment in droplet-flame survival, especially near-limit behaviour. Outcome: Follow-on droplet campaign examined fuel mixtures and stricter diluent controls, extending extinction-limit evidence beyond FLEX's single-fuel scope. Fuel: Methanol / ethanol / heptane mixtures (droplets). Atmosphere: 18% O2 at 80 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Quiescent (still chamber). Hardware: ISS · CIR · MDCA. Years: Follow-on to FLEX (approx.).

Flame Extinguishment Experiment – 2 (FLEX-2) — published finding: Mixture droplets show distinct cool-flame and survival windows not present in single-fuel droplets (published summaries describe these regimes) [4].
Flame Extinguishment Experiment – 2 (FLEX-2) — published finding: Extends the extinction-limit map relevant to gaseous-suppression and atmospherically diluted environments [4].

Flame Extinguishment Experiment – 2 (FLEX-2) variables swept: Fuel mixtures; O₂; Diluent type & amount; Droplet size. Measurements recorded: Diameter history; Extinction diameter; Cool-flame observations; Burning rate. Fuel: Methanol / ethanol / heptane mixtures (droplets). Atmosphere: 18% O2 at 80 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Quiescent (still chamber).
Flame Extinguishment Experiment – 2 (FLEX-2) materials/samples tested: Methanol; Ethanol; Heptane; Binary mixtures of the above.

Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) (BRE). Objective: Estimate the burning rates of solid materials by placing a gas burner flame that reproduces the heat-feedback of a burning solid — turning material flammability into a well-controlled gas-flame study. Outcome: Published summaries describe gaseous burner flames set to emulate a burning solid surface in still air, so material-property-based flammability can be probed without dealing with sample variability. Fuel: Gaseous (emulating solid burning). Atmosphere: 21% O2 at 101 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Quiescent (still atmosphere). Hardware: ISS · CIR · ACME modular chamber hardware. Years: 2010s (approx.).

Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) — published finding: Provides a materials-flammability bridge for spacecraft atmospheres without burning solid samples directly — usable as a proxy for the crew-environment relevance ranking (see Mission Fit) [5].
Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) — published finding: Still-atmosphere burning-rate data directly inform the ventilation-dependence of spacecraft fire risk [5].

Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) variables swept: Emulated solid material properties; O₂; Pressure; Still vs forced flow. Measurements recorded: Burning rate; Flame strength; Extinction onset; Heat release (reported by O₂ consumption). Fuel: Gaseous (emulating solid burning). Atmosphere: 21% O2 at 101 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Quiescent (still atmosphere).
Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) materials/samples tested: Gas flames emulating solid-fuel burning rates (material properties input).

Cooled Laminar Diffusion Flames (CLD Flame) (CLD-FLAME). Objective: Develop and study a laminar diffusion flame in which soot formation can be controlled (via a cooled burner), informing how flames produce smoke and how smoke generation limits might be designed. Outcome: Published summaries describe soot formation and elimination in a cooled, co-flowing diffusion flame, linking burner temperature and dilution to soot production. Fuel: Gaseous hydrocarbon (ethylene / fuel gas, approx.). Atmosphere: 21% O2 at 101 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Co-flowing laminar diffusion flame. Hardware: ISS · CIR · ACME modular chamber hardware. Years: 2010s (approx.).

Cooled Laminar Diffusion Flames (CLD Flame) — published finding: Soot-free (or soot-controlled) diffusion flames were demonstrated, informing how flame temperature and dilution drive smoke production [5].
Cooled Laminar Diffusion Flames (CLD Flame) — published finding: Furnishes smoke-generation evidence relevant to the SAME/R-particulate line (detection calibration) [5].

Cooled Laminar Diffusion Flames (CLD Flame) variables swept: Burner temperature; Fuel/diluent mix; Co-flow setting. Measurements recorded: Soot volume fraction; Flame structure video; Temperature field. Fuel: Gaseous hydrocarbon (ethylene / fuel gas, approx.). Atmosphere: 21% O2 at 101 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Co-flowing laminar diffusion flame.
Cooled Laminar Diffusion Flames (CLD Flame) materials/samples tested: Hydrocarbon gas fuel (ethylene-class, approximate); N₂ / diluent streams.

Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) (E-FIELD). Objective: Use flame ions themselves as an actuator: apply an electric field to spherically rounded microgravity diffusion flames to test flame-shape and soot control, and to mimic partial-gravity dynamics. Outcome: Published summaries describe electric-field forcing of ions within buoyancy-free flames, driving flame-shape and motion change analogous to partial-gravity effects. Fuel: Methane (gas). Atmosphere: 21% O2 at 101 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Quiescent laminar diffusion flame. Hardware: ISS · CIR · ACME modular chamber hardware (with electric-field electrodes). Years: 2010s (approx.).

text: Flame Design (FLAME-DESIGN). Objective: Test the hypothesis that soot production in flames depends on the flame's oxidative/dilution environment (not just chemistry), directly informing how elevated-O₂ atmospheres change spacecraft fire risk. Outcome: Published summaries describe O₂-enriched and diluent-swept diffusion flames that decouple soot formation from flame temperature and stoichiometry in microgravity. Fuel: Ethylene / fuel gas (approx.). Atmosphere: 21% O2 at 101 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Laminar diffusion flame with enriched-O₂/diluent flow. Hardware: ISS · CIR · ACME modular chamber hardware. Years: 2020s (approx.).
Flame Design — published finding: Directly probes the elevated-O₂ regime — the atmospheric knob that makes materials more flammable on a Moon Base (per the plan to use ≥30% O₂ atmospheres there) [5].
Flame Design — published finding: Provides smoke-point evidence at O₂ enrichment relevant to upcoming spacecraft atmospheres [5].

Flame Design variables swept: O₂ enrichment; Diluent (He/N₂); Fuel flow; Smoke point. Measurements recorded: Smoke point; Soot production; Heat-release behavior; Flame structure. Fuel: Ethylene / fuel gas (approx.). Atmosphere: 21% O2 at 101 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Laminar diffusion flame with enriched-O₂/diluent flow.
Flame Design materials/samples tested: Ethylene-class hydrocarbon gas fuels; O₂-enriched and He/N₂-diluent atmospheres.

Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) (CFI). Objective: Dedicated cool-flame droplet-burning study — understand low-temperature chemistry regimes that can burn invisibly ('cool flames') after visible flame extinction. Outcome: Published summaries describe continued droplet cool-flame research using the MDCA, extending FLEX-2's cool-flame discovery toward a dedicated investigation. Fuel: Heptane-class fuel (droplets). Atmosphere: 18% O2 at 80 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Quiescent droplet burning. Hardware: ISS · CIR · MDCA (per droplet-combustion line). Years: 2015–2019 (approx.).

Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) — published finding: Cool-flame combustion — a combustion mode invisible to the eye and to many alarms — is a confirmed microgravity phenomenon with real fire-detection implication [7].
Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) — published finding: Extends FLEX's extinction-limit evidence toward next-generation droplet fire models [7].

Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) variables swept: Fuel identity/mixtures; O₂; Pressure; Droplet diameter. Measurements recorded: Droplet history; Cool-flame diagnostics; Extinction diameters. Fuel: Heptane-class fuel (droplets). Atmosphere: 18% O2 at 80 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Quiescent droplet burning.
Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) materials/samples tested: Heptane-class liquid fuels (possibly mixtures).

Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G) (CFI-G). Objective: Spherical-burner cool-flame study using the highest-O₂ atmospheres in microgravity, probing the fuel-oxidation chemistry that spans visible flame double-diffusion through cool-flame regimes. Outcome: The challenge text describes chamber atmospheres of N₂ + fuel gas with an O₂/N₂ mixture supplied by the spherical burner reaching up to ≈85% O₂ — the highest-O₂ microgravity combustion tests reported. Fuel: Gaseous fuel (e.g. propane) + O₂/N₂ burner stream. Atmosphere: 85% O2 at —. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Low-speed flow from a spherical burner. Hardware: ISS · combustion chamber with spherical burner. Years: 2020s (approx.).

text: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) (SPICE). Objective: Determine how smoke points (the fuel flow / O₂ condition at which a flame first puts out soot) change in microgravity, providing a soot-production baseline for spacecraft flames. Outcome: Published summaries measure smoke points of gas flames in microgravity co-flow, showing smoke-point behaviour differs from Earth-bound correlations used in design. Fuel: Hydrocarbon gas jets (methane / ethylene class, approx.). Atmosphere: 21% O2 at 101 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Co-flow duct (low flow). Hardware: ISS · MSG fan-driven flow duct (SPICE hardware, shared by BASS/SLICE). Years: 2010s (approx.).

text: Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE) (SLICE). Objective: Measure flame liftoff and stability boundaries in microgravity — the conditions under which flames detach from their supply or restabilize, important for understanding fire spread along fuel lines. Outcome: Published summaries track flame liftoff, stability and reattachment behaviour in microgravity co-flow across a range of jet velocities — the same hardware lineage as SPICE. Fuel: Methane / ethylene gas jets. Atmosphere: 21% O2 at 101 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Co-flow duct (variable flow). Hardware: ISS · MSG fan-driven flow duct (SPICE hardware lineage). Years: 2010s (approx.).

Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE) — published finding: Liftoff/stability evidence in microgravity differs from Earth-consistent correlations (published summaries describe the deviation) [9].
Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE) — published finding: Feeds the ventilation-and-flow chapter of spacecraft fire models (how flame attachment changes with airflow) [9].

Fuel: Methane / ethylene gas jets. Atmosphere: 21% O2 at 101 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Co-flow duct (variable flow).
Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE) materials/samples tested: Methane; Ethylene jets; Optional dilution gas sets.

Objective: Re-use the SAME-line detection hardware to characterize ambient spacecraft dust and aerosols — a feasibility test of the instrument's broader use beyond combustion smoke detection. Outcome: Published summaries use a smoke-detection instrument (the SAME family) on ambient cabin dust instead of combustion smoke, characterizing dust particle sizes in microgravity. Fuel: Ambient ISS dust (no combustion fuel). Atmosphere: — O2 at 101 kPa. Gravity: Microgravity. Airflow: Quiescent ambient sampling.
